utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Wednesday, 21st of May, 2008. Good afternoon to the witness, to the Defence counsel, to the accused, to everyone assisting us in this courtroom, and to the Prosecution. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. We'll start with the Defence counsel, and I believe that Mr. Kovacic will be the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As you have told yesterday, I'm going to put a few questions to you. All of them in connection with the topics that were raised in your examination-in-chief, and I'm talking only about very short three topics. In your testimony so far -- I apologise. Have you received a document? Now you're going to receive it I can see. In your testimony so far, on the first day, on page 95, line 7 - I'm stating this just for the record - you mentioned a person by the name of Jakov Binenfeld. You said that he was the owner of the VIP agency and that agency performed a job for you, and the job in question was the third census of refugees and displaced persons. Dr. Rebic, let me remind you that my cross-examination is going to differ from the examination in -- so far. We speak the same language, and in order to make the lives of the interpreters easier, we should make a short break between my questions and your answer. My first question is this: Did you have an occasion to meet this person, Binenfeld, in person?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, according to what you know about him, would that be a person of high moral standards, enjoying a high reputation in society?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, this person has high professional qualities, a capable businessman at the time. At the time he had his own agency, the name of the agency was VIP. It was the best agency at the time in the Republic of Croatia and it was for that reason that I, in agreement with UNHCR, or better say on their instruction, I chose him. It was a private agency, and UNHCR preferred private agency over any government agency. As far as his moral qualities are concerned, I wouldn't go into that because I don't have any information about that. In my view, he was a good man, a good businessman. I had several occasions to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you perhaps learn from Mr. Binenfeld himself or in any other way that he had been a very active and highly positioned officer in the Zagreb Jewish community?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was active in the Jewish community of Zagreb. He was not very much engaged, but he was engaged in the Jewish community, and in that respect he was my friend, because I -- I like Jewish people. I speak Hebrew. I read Hebrew. I often go to Israel. This coming Sunday I have to go to Israel. And that's why I socialised with Binenfeld, but this had nothing to do with my decision to choose his agency for the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that part of your decision. I have no doubt about your right to choose whomever you want based on whatever information you have. I'm more interested in Binenfeld himself. Did you have an occasion to learn that the same gentleman, Jakov Binenfeld, had organised, i.e., had carried out the organisation of the humanitarian convoys in the course of 1992 and 1993. And like all the other humanitarian convoys, those convoys were of twofold nature. One of the purposes was to take people from occupied Sarajevo, and second purpose was to bring humanitarian aid to Sarajevo. Do you know that he was a person who participated in the organisation of these convoys? But let me rephrase my question to avoid any objections. First of all, do you know that he was involved in that project?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was involved in that project, and sometimes he would come to the office to receive information with regard to the situation in Sarajevo and in Bosnia and Herzegovina in general. He wanted to know how to get there, how to help and so on and so forth. He wanted to receive information from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And my next question arises from your answer. Are you aware of the fact that convoys of that sort did actually go to Sarajevo and come back?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several convoys took humanitarian aid to Sarajevo and took Jews out of occupied Sarajevo, and this was done with his help.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm not interested in anything else at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Trial Chamber held that when a subject has not been dealt with during the examination-in-chief, the Defence is perfectly entitled to deal with that subject, but the time used will be deduced from the time allocated to the Defence for its own examination-in-chief, and since we heard nothing about convoys, the time you will spend dealing with that will be deducted from the time you've been granted for your own examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course this is your decision. I will abide by that, but if you will allow me just two sentences. The witness did mention this person, Jakov Binenfeld, in the examination-in-chief. He explained why he had chosen that agency, and in my view one of the factors which was just confirmed by the witness was the moral standing and the professionalism of that person. This is what I wanted to verify. I had to ask him about the convoys in order to find out whether that person did have those moral -- that moral integrity. I believe that the questions are connected and that they would fall under the sphere of the cross-examination. And second of all, and an additional reason why I'm asking this witness about the convoy, and that was only my last question, was the fact that on my list, 92 bis witnesses, I have that person and his statement about those convoys and Praljak's role and assistance with the organisation of these convoys. If you are taking that time off my time, then I believe that only the last question should be taken off my time, that question about the convoys. Yes. My client is reminding me that there is a document to that effect. In order to avoid wasting any more time, with your leave I would like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, my learned friend Karnavas showed you amongst other things document D 02610. You have it in my binder which consists of only two documents. This is your letter. You told us about this letter. You're asking the Ministry of Culture and education to provide you with the information about the number of children included in regular education because this is what you had been requested to do by the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We've already spoken about that? If you look at the number of this document and the date, and could you please look at my next document which is 3D 01036. So first let's identify the document. This is a letter to the government of the Republic of Croatia, i.e., to the office of the refugees and displaced persons. The address is the address of your office. The date is 18th of January. The signatory of this document is Vesna Giradi-Jurkic, Master of Science, the then Minister of Education. In the first line of this text pursuant to your letter number 01904, if we look at the number on the document that was shown to you yesterday my question, Dr. Rebic, would be this: Do you agree with me that this is obviously the answer to your request dated 12 January?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, although I see this document after 12 years today, but I remember it well, and the number 32.000 students, refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina were regular students within our education system out of whom 25.000 in primary schools and 6.000 in secondary schools. This number -- these numbers correspond to the numbers brought by the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons in their reports based on the registration for refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. In order to avoid wasting time you have now read item 1 of this letter. You started talking about numbers here and this confirms what you said yesterday not only with regard to the figures but also with regard to the system. It says here that the children were included in the regular school system. That's what we're interested in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Would you then agree that this is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now I will move on to another topic that was raised by you. On two occasions during your testimony so far you've mentioned in broader terms the cooperation with your -- between your office and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, some of which had previously been owned by the JNA. You wanted to use them for refugees because they had all the necessary infrastructure. And then yesterday, towards the end of the day, you mentioned a situation when you had been given an HV aircraft to transport you to Split because you had some problems with refugees there. My question is as follows: Is it true that your office had various aspects of cooperation with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic. Our office had different forms of cooperation with the MOD, not only when it came to taking over some of the facilities, military facilities, i.e., barracks, that we needed to accommodate refugees because they had all the necessary infrastructure and they were not at the time required by the Croatian army. Besides these facilities still had some personnel, civilian personnel, such as cooks and cleaning staff. So in that respect we had a logistical support. I remember Mr. Vukina from the MOD who was of a huge help to me when it came to logistics and the accommodation of refugees and displaced persons, and in light of the fact that at the very beginning the army was well-organised in terms of supplies and accommodation. So we had a lot of help from the MOD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. Dr. Rebic, tell us, please, whether these were the only topics that you dealt with in your frequent contacts, or whether -- or were there any occasions when the Ministry of Defence or the HV helped with some incidents, with some complex situations when you had to deal with the situation immediately if not yesterday? You did not have your own people, so did you sometimes turn to the Ministry of Defence for help because the Ministry of Defence obviously had personnel, organisation, and equipment? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This help primarily concerned logistics. I'm talking about accommodating refugees and organising refugee centres. This is all the help that we received from the MOD, logistical support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Within the MOD did you have any cooperation with the information and propaganda department? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, I did not have any contacts with them. They could receive information from our office if they asked for it, because our information was public and accessible to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During your contacts with the Ministry of Defence did you ever meet General Praljak in person?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met General Praljak and I remember that meeting. It was very early on. I may not remember the exact date, but I believe that it was in February or March 1992 when we had some problems at the office. So together with Mrs. Rukavina -- I believe that was her name. Mrs. Rukavina was the head of the regional office for refugees and displaced persons in the city of Zagreb. We had some problems with accommodation and the attitude of some younger people towards the army and the refugees, and he was very helpful in dealing with all these problems. I remember that Mrs. Rukavina and I met in a very modest room and that -- that is when I met a very modest person who gave his whole heart to serving the Croatian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, who are you referring to when you say a modest person?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm referring to Mr. Praljak. Later on Mrs. Rukavina, who was a very decent and honest woman had nothing but the words of praise about him. Her son fought in the army near Sisak, and at the time Mr. Praljak was the head of that defence. She had only the word of -- words of praise for his firmness and his fair dealings towards his co-fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When Mrs. Rukavina told you about the positions around Sisak would I be -- would I jog your memory if I told you that this was Sunja?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right there. It was Sunja. Sunja at the time was theatre of major conflicts between the JNA, the Serb paramilitaries, and our own Croatian army, and our lads fought very hard to repel the -- the Yugoslav People's Army and not to let them through to -- all the way to Zagreb, because this is not very far from Zagreb for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that Mrs. Rukavina told you how the army and General Praljak helped her in her job. Do you -- do you perhaps remember an event which took place in 1992, very early in the year, when Mate Granic, as the vice-prime minister promised the European Monitoring Mission that he would give them the hotel in the Jakomir neighbourhood of Zagreb? Let me just try and jog your memory and tell you that that hotel at the time accommodated refugees from Vukovar, and when they were told that they would be moved or at least there was an intention to do so, they rebelled. They didn't want to move, and if I remember the whole incident well and the papers that I read about the incident, the then mayor, Marina Matulovic Dropulic, intervened and the whole situation was compounded because the city had proposed the refugees from Vukovar to be accommodated in the 7th -- 7 secretaries of SKOJ facility, the whole thing escalated, and then the army proposed some of the hospital facilities in the old Vlaska street in Zagreb. Is that the incident that you had in mind when you said that there were some problems?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly that one, but I do remember that particular incident. Unfortunately, this happened on Christmas, and it was really a very sad thing that refugees from Vukovar whom the Serbs had expelled from their own Croatian homes and killed many of them, all these people were very stressed out. They were already accommodated in the facility before the office, my office, was established, because they had had been expelled from Vukovar in the course of the month of September, October, and November 1991. And then these facilities were required by the army, which means that the refugees from Vukovar had to be moved from that facility. Both refugees and displaced persons were very sensitive, and they did not respond to any such attempt to move them lightly. And then Mr. Granic got involved because the Office for Refugees Displaced and Persons had started functioning only before Christmas. That's why Mr. Granic played a somewhat bigger role. He personally spoke to all these people and an agreement was reached for them to be transferred, some of them to Vlaska Street or to the premises of the former military hospital, and the others were moved to Kozhnice. This is what you mentioned under the name of 7 secretaries of SKOJ. In Kozhnice they had very good facility, very good accommodation. I don't know -- I don't remember now whether this was a military facility or whether this was a facility that belonged to the city of Zagreb. It seems to me that the facility did belong to the city of Zagreb. In any case, it was in good order, and later on we did not have any more problems with the refugees there. They -- they made themselves comfortable both in the hospital and in the Kozhnice facility. I visited them in both these places in Vlaska and in Kozhnice, and I even celebrated the holy mass on Christmas in Kozhnice. Actually it wasn't on Christmas, it was New Year's, a week after Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just to verify something. You said that it was around Christmas. Was it '92?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was 1991.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 1991, because Vukovar fell in 1991 towards the end of October, on the 21st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And also you mentioned the hospital in Vlaska Street in Zagreb, or at least some of the facilities there. Was that before the war property of JNA, and then pursuant to a government decree it was under the control of the Ministry of Defence when the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Kovacic. The property of the JNA was taken over by the Croatian army once Croatia gained independence -- independence, and it is only logical. The HV did not -- did not need the hospital, which was very large, and that's why they decided and agreed to hand over a large part of that facility to the refugees from Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we now summarise and say that in light of all these contacts with the Ministry of Defence, their help and their property, could you please just briefly in two sentences, because we don't have any more time, could you briefly tell us whether the overall cooperation with the Ministry of Defence concerning the displaced persons and later on refugees, was it good? Was the Ministry of Defence willing to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cooperation was good. It was very useful to our office and to refugees and displaced persons, and if the Croatian army had not helped us, we would have had much more difficulties when it came to looking after refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. Referring to the incident concerning the displaced persons from Vukovar, do you remember that at one point General Praljak became directly involved in the attempt to convince these people from Vukovar that they should cooperate and that they should move as they were asked to do? Did you have any information about this?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that because on that occasion I didn't visit the facility myself. It was Deputy Prime Minister Granic who visited it. That's why I don't remember, because I wasn't actually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Rebic. Those were all my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with respect to my calculation of time, I wish to add to my previous arguments that refugees from Sarajevo were mentioned during the examination-in-chief yesterday, and document 2D 00454 was put to the witness. For this reason, I submit that all my questions, including the ones concerning the convoy, did have to do with the examination-in-chief. The Defence did raise that issue, and it is my standpoint that my questions were within the -- that framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. The Chamber will rule on this particular point. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. I wish good day to you and to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Dr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am an attorney at law from Zagreb appearing for Milivoj Petkovic. I will put a brief question to you concerning the convention on the status of refugees, and after that I will put a few questions to you about a document put to you by the Defence of Jadranko Prlic which Their Honours were greatly interested in. My first question concerns the convention on the status of refugees. Could you please take a look at my document 4D 01233. In this document, if we can look at it together, it says that the government of the Republic of Croatia issued a decision on the publication of multi-lateral international agreements, and it says in the introduction that the Republic of Croatia, as of the 8th of October, 1991, was through succession a party to the follow international agreements, and under number 35 it mentions the convention on the status of refugees of 1951, and under item 37 the protocol on the legal status of refugees from 1967. Dr. Rebic, could you please confirm to us -- well, can you first of all tell us what this date, the 8th of October, 1991, refers to? Why is that the date when Croatia acceded to these international treaties?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, that was the date when the Croatian parliament -- well, I can't remember precisely, but I know that the date was of importance for the Republic of Croatia, and there were even proposals that it should become a public holiday. I know that the parliament made an important decision on that date. Can you jog my memory and tell me what it was?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll jog your memory. Was it then that the parliament adopted the decision that Croatia should become an independent country?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right. I thought at first that this happened in June, but you are right, it happened in October.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In June the decision was made but then there was a three-month moratorium, which is why the 8th of October, 1991, is the date when independence was declared. Can you confirm, Dr. Rebic, that as of the first day of its existence as an independent state, Croatia was a party to these international treaties and agreements?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document we discussed most yesterday bears the number P 10048. Dr. Rebic, please pay attention to the monitor. I believe that this will be sufficient for the purposes of my examination. This is a document concerning the taking in of 500 persons from Mostar. Do you remember yesterday's discussion of that document? In the course of yesterday's examination, I received the impression that you did not understand what it was that Their Honours did not understand in connection with this document. Am I right in thinking that you were confused?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I really was confused, because I didn't understand what sort of clarification was expected of me. My impression was that Their Honours were not aware of the geographical relations between Bosnia-Herzegovina and third countries and that perhaps they were not fully aware of the geography.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, as you are not a lawyer, I'm not going to ask you the same sort of questions about this document that I would ask a fellow lawyer, but I believe I can put some questions to you that you will be able to answer. Please tell us to whom was this document addressed? To whom was it sent?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, as is evident, was sent to the police station in Vrgorac, to the border police and to the border crossing, Banja Vrgorac. The document was primarily addressed to the border police so that based on this document they could let through persons who wanted to go from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to third countries, and to do that they had to cross the territory of the Republic of Croatia. This made it possible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm sorry to interrupt. Following what you said, for your information, sir, I would just like to mention that the Trial Chamber went to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have personally been there on many occasions, so this is just for your personal information. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, please look at the following: On the -- at the bottom of the page it also says that copies were sent to the Ministry of the Interior, the migration unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite understandably because the document was sent to the border police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, as this document was addressed to the police, does this mean, in fact, that the police addressed your office and asked your opinion on the request of these 500 persons to enter Croatia and to gain temporary residence in Croatia? So my question is: Did you send this document to the police because you received an inquiry from the police?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, evidently, yes, because otherwise the police would not be allowed to let these people into the Republic of Croatia without this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It follows further from this document that your office gave its agreement to have these persons granted entry and permanent residence in Croatia. So it follows from this that some other organ actually issued the approval for their entry and temporary residence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees gave its agreement and also gave its agreement that for a time these refugees, until such time as the third entity, this was evidently the UNHCR, could accommodate them in the countries to which they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware under Croatian legislation, or maybe you can see it from this document, after the granting of approval for the entry and -- or, rather, was it the Ministry of the Interior which granted approval for these persons to enter the country with your agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not the Ministry of the Interior. It was the office that decided on this, and we informed the ministry of that, because refugees came under the authority of the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees not under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior as happens in some other countries.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because they didn't want to take them in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. So these persons did not have refugee status; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It follows from this document that these persons had the status of refugees staying in Croatia based on a temporary residence permit.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but because they hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina, they had de facto care because of their refugee status whether it was recognised de jure or not. De facto the Republic of Croatia had to provide them with everything it provided for refugees. We could not leave them out in the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's clear. So these persons are entering Croatia as foreigners based on temporary residence permit, and they were accommodated in the camp in Gasinci; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are there grounds to conclude then that you participated in the issuing of this document, because these persons were being taken care of in a refugee centre?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And there was an UNHCR office in Gasinci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. About three times the interpreters have asked to make a pause after you've spoken. Perhaps you've not heard it, but it's really very trying on them, and it will be very nice if you could try to comply. I very well know how difficult it is. I have all the understanding, but please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In our language we didn't hear -- on our channel we didn't hear these interpreter interventions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rebic, I'm not taking for granted that you're familiar with Croatian legislation and regulations, but I do have to ask you the following: Under Article 22, and you don't have this document before you, of the Croatian law on the movement and stay of refugees, I have it translated for Their Honours, and if they wish to see it in English it's ready to be distributed. For the purposes of my cross-examination, it will be sufficient for me to say, and this document was used in e-court during the examination-in-chief, 4D 01232. In Article 22, Mr. Rebic, please listen, the Croatian law states that a foreigner can stay in Croatia based on five legal grounds. I will list them. The first is temporary residence, the second is extended residence, the third is residence with a business visa, the fourth is residence pursuant to approved permanent residence, and the third is pursuant to recognised refugee status. Were you aware in principle that foreigners could stay in Croatia on various legal bases?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was primarily aware of the fact that anyone who came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Vojvodina or from Serbia also, had the right to stay in the Republic of Croatia with the permission of our office, which recognised refugee status or displaced person status for three months, six months, a year, or on a temporary basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So your office made decisions on one of these legal bases for the stay of foreigners in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: A person could also stay in Croatia due to temporary residence, which was decided by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Mr. Rebic, are you aware whether residence in Croatia on one legal ground excluded the possibility of a person simultaneously staying in Croatia based on another legal ground?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to this document now, 10048. That's P 10048, and you will see it on your screen. It's to do with the persons arriving from Mostar. And in the introduction it says in the preamble that these persons are arriving in Croatia and they are being granted temporary residence. That's one legal ground on which the MUP decides. That's in the first paragraph. And in the third paragraph it says: "Pursuant to this" -- look at the last line, and I emphasise "Pursuant to this these persons do not have the right to request or obtain refugee status." That was the reason I asked whether one legal ground excluded the others. So these two words, "Pursuant to this," or "In accordance with this," these persons do not have the right to ask for refugee status, and the reason is that their residence in Croatia has already been granted on another legal basis, which is temporary residence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just again so the record is clear on this, and I think just now is a perfect illustration of the problem, we continue to object to leading questions in this context. This is a friendly witness, a witness entirely friendly to Ms. Alaburic. He has given no adverse evidence to her client, and the Defence has been given an unfair advantage by being able to put leading questions, subjective direct questions to the witness just as the one just given. I ask the Chamber to look at the transcript, look at the question. That is a clearly leading question being put to a non-adverse witness, and Prosecution continues to object to this practice. As the Chamber may know we've filed a -- we've made a written motion -- filed a written motion on this topic today, and this illustrates the point very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course this matter has been subject to a motion filed by the Prosecution. It's trite to say, however, that the proposition put forward by the Prosecution is entirely novel or very largely novel at least, at the very least, in this Tribunal. Your Honour, it's a matter for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I interrupt, but this is now pending before us and the Defence will have a chance to answer. I do not think it conducive to any good if we discuss it now. The Chamber has taken note of the objection, and I think we leave it at that. I would suggest that we do not take more time for a discussion that could go on for a long time, appreciating your -- what you're saying. It's not that it's wrong, but I think it is not conducive to our work at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, so be it. We will respond in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And I would like to inform everyone that the witness told us that he was going to Israel this weekend, and in order to make sure that he doesn't have to come back next week, let's try to avoid wasting time. And as my learned friend -- fellow Judge said the question is a pending one, and I would like to invite Ms. Alaburic, if possible, to put neutral questions to the witness just like the Judges do when they put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your instruction, Your Honours. I will do my best to put neutral questions to the extent possible. If Dr. Rebic were a lawyer, I would put different questions, but if a lawyer is putting questions to layperson about legal matters, then I believe that a different approach is in order, and --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. If I may say, Your Honours, I can't be led by anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness, for your answer. I already said this for other witnesses. Given the quality of the witnesses, it seems that it is very difficult to manipulate witnesses. Please proceed, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It hasn't been my intention to manipulate anybody. I believe that we will benefit most from correct answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, I remind you that we have left it off with the fact that these persons could not ask for refugee status because they had been permitted to stay in Croatia based on some other legal grounds, and in this particular case it was prolonged stay. Tell us, please, whether the status was decided by the Republic of Croatia or the person arriving in Croatia by way of submitting one or another kind of request.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons had a say in that and they decided that in keeping with the situation that brought the person to Croatia and their own will. If that person requested a refugee status in the Republic of Croatia, then that person would be granted that status. If they arrived in the Croatian -- in the Republic of Croatia with an express request to stay in Croatia only temporarily because they had a place to stay in a third country, then we had no reason not to respect the person's will and granted a temporary stay. We did not force such a person to stay in Croatia any longer than they were willing to stay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, for example, a refugee from Bosnia and Herzegovina, a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina who was fleeing from war, could they be given the refugee status in several countries, for example, in Croatia, Great Britain, France, or was there a rule that regulated that differently?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practical terms somebody who enjoys -- enjoyed refugee status in Croatia and then went on to Croatia and when leaving the Republic of Croatia they did --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, and left for Germany.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when leaving Croatia they did not cancel their status in Croatia and requested a status in Germany. So that person would have dual refugee status, but it was of no use because they could not enjoy benefits in both countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, in that case we're talking about manipulation. Tell me, please, was it not the rule that the refugee status could only be enjoyed in one country, and if the status is obtained, for example, in Croatia, then only through this seat and manipulation were you able to acquire the same status in a third country. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please now explain for the Trial Chamber, Dr. Rebic, if somebody transited through the Republic of Croatia with an intention to go to a third country where they wanted to be granted a refugee status, would obtaining the refugee status in Croatia impede on that original intention?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know, because that third country would hardly be able to know that that person had already been granted the refugee status in Croatia. At that time, there was -- the communication means were not as developed as they are today. There was no e-mails, postal services, and after all, it was war. There were a lot of refugees who moved all the time from one state to another. They would go. They would come back. There was a lot of movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Under the assumption that the documentation is in order, that it was very hard to conceal any information, would it be logic -- logical for a person leaving for a third country and applying for the refugee status there to only pass through Croatia in transit, because otherwise they would not be able to be granted a refugee status in a third country?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be logical for Croatia to receive transit passengers from Bosnia-Herzegovina who wanted to be granted a refugee status in a third country?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question, Witness. In this courtroom many of us are more or less specialised in refugee statuses, and the questions that you were asked helped to understand clearly the refugee status. But I would like to put this question for you. A person that for instance obtains insurances or guarantee letters that Denmark, for instance, is going to grant him a refugee status, your office at that point, or the government of Croatia at the time, were you doing everything in your power to allow this refugee to go to Denmark, or was he going to be granted a refugee status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that most often it was the refugees themselves who organised their own departure through third countries, for example, Denmark, in cooperation with the UNHCR. As far as I remember, Croatia did not organise such departures to third countries. As I say, this is as far as I can remember. It would have been very difficult, because Croatia could not organise a convoy or transportation of any sort to take them first to Slovenia and then further on. It was just inconceivable at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand that a situation was quite complex, but let's suppose that we have a person who comes from Mostar. That person no longer has any papers for whatever reason. That person comes to your office, is taken care of by your office because -- and he does not have any papers. He does not have a passport of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but let's say he has to take the plane to go to London, and he has to go through Zagreb and there are some border crossings that he has to go through. Is your office going to give him a letter, a safe-passage letter, enabling that person to go to England, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such person would receive from the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons or, better say for one of the regional offices and there were a total of 21 of them all over Croatia, such a person would receive documents that we used to call transit visas, and based on those documents such person would be received by third country, for example, Denmark, because that document provided with a status of refugee. Those papers showed quite clearly that the person had fled from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that it requested a transit visa in Croatia. That person did not have any other documents for us either, and we could only believe persons -- the person, what they said, because they did not provide us with any documents, no passport, no birth certificate or anything. Some of these people had all their documents burnt and all their family killed. They didn't have anything on them. They just presented themselves as persons without any documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott, you have four hours and 15 minutes, or four hours and 20 minutes, but we have another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question -- or two follow-up questions after the President's question. Please try to be very concise when answering. Which minister did your -- did your office depend on? Were you under the Minister of Foreign Affairs or another ministry, or were you under direct responsibility of the head of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons was established by the government of the Republic of Croatia as its instrument, as it's new ministry of sorts, and it was not under any other ministry. It was reporting directly to the government at the time. It was Dr. Mate Granic who was the vice-prime minister in charge of social issues. In other words, our office had a direct link of communication with the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question. The mandate of your office was to accommodate and take care of refugees and displaced persons. Did you have the power to grant refugee status to individuals who were outside of Croatia, or did your power, your authority in that respect, only apply to those individuals who were already in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our authority applied to all people, to all those who were already in the Republic of Croatia and had already requested a refugee status, as well as those persons who were arriving from a different state, in this particular case, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and came to us to request refugee status. We were the only office that was able and allowed to grant that status to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott, you have the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll be distributing some papers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, to counsel, to all those in and around the courtroom, and especially Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm not sure, I've been thinking back over the last couple of days and I'm not -- I cannot recall whether I've ever cross-examined a priest before. I'm just wondering, do I need to have any sort of special dispensation or any special permission to do that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is not a confession, is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. We'll see. We will see. If we can just touch a bit on -- a little bit more on your agency and, in fact, to follow up on some of the questions that Judge Mindua put to you, and some of them may be similar, but perhaps we can capture as much of this information in one spot. It may ultimately assist. You became involved with the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Croatia essentially at its inception; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we're just touching on the relationship with the Croatian government. Do I understand correctly, sir, that in terms of a superior, if the person who we might consider in colloquial terms your boss, is it correct that that would have been Mate Granic who, at that time, I believe was both the Minister of Foreign Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but at the time, at the very beginning, he was not the Minister of Foreign Affairs. He was only deputy prime minister responsible for social issues. And since the office was basically concerned with social issues, he would have been our boss, as you put it, and through him we would also be reporting to the government. It would not have been fair for me to contact the prime minister directly, bypassing Mr. Granic's authority. That would not have been fair, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, you're absolutely correct. Later -- at a point later in time Mr. Granic also became -- or became the deputy prime minister during the time you were still at ODPR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, what you were going to ask me I believe is that he later on became the Minister of Foreign Affairs. He already was a deputy prime minister. Am I right in correcting you there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. How often did you have dealings with Mate Granic as your boss? Did you have any sort of regular weekly meeting with him? Did you have to report to him your schedule, your work plan? What sort of relationship did you have with Mr. Granic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the OTP are meaning either me personally as the head of the office or together with my deputy or secretary or some other person who was in charge of the issues that we wanted to brief Mr. Granic about. We would go to meet him. Those briefings of ours would take place several times a week. There were times when we would meet on a daily basis because that's what the situation called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. And during the period -- we're going to be focusing primarily on 1992 into -- into 1994. During that time period at the ODPR, who was your principal deputy or right hand, if you will?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Cepin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the position held by Dr. Zoric?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Damir Zoric was the Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were the three of you, you, Dr. Rebic, Mr. Cepin, and Mr. Zoric -- Dr. Zoric, can we accurately understand then that the three of you were considered the three senior officials in the agency?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would say the most involved in the work of the office, but Mr. Cepin, my deputy, joined us a bit later when the job outgrew the current personnel, and that's why the government offered me to take on a deputy who helped in dealing with the issues concerning the main office, the regional offices, and all the issues that concerned refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, building on that in terms of your dealing with other offices, let me ask you. As you know, there came to be an office for displaced persons and refugees, an agency by the same name in Herceg-Bosna, and can you tell us who in your office, perhaps you, but who in your office had the principal contacts or dealings with the ODPR outside the ODPR HVO?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ODPR had contacts with Sarajevo through Mrs. Omersoftic. Mrs. Omersoftic arrived in mid-1992 in Zagreb and asked me to brief her about the job of taking in displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, just as Mr. Karnavas did, with my apology in advance, there may be times when I will unfortunately interrupt you because of the time limitations that we have to operate under. Let me restate my question. Perhaps it wasn't clear. I was not talking about the agency to deal with displaced persons of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question to you concerned the Office of Displaced Persons and Refugees that was set up by the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, in Mostar, and my question to you, who among your office in Zagreb, who had most of the dealings and contact with the ODPR HVO?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That office, the one on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was set up, started operating a little later than the similar office in Sarajevo. Consequently, pursuant to an agreement between the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was determined that the Republic of Croatia should provide logistical support to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Sarajevo, to the Bosniak Muslim side, and also to the Bosnian Croatian side. At that time it was decided that the Republic of Croatia would help to organise such an office on the territory controlled by the HVO. This was done, and they just like Mrs. Omersoftic came to obtain the basic information and instructions on how to go about setting up such an office and then they set one up in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Let me thank you for that. Let me ask my question again a third time. Who, who -- the people in your office, yourself perhaps, Mr. Cepin, Dr. Zoric, who in your office in ODPR Croatia, who had the dealing -- principal dealings with ODPR HVO, and who did you deal with -- who was the person or persons that the ODPR HVO that you had your dealings with?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three of us participated in that. Most often I as the head of the office. They would come to see me and inform me about the situation, just as Mrs. Omersoftic did to inform me about the situation in Sarajevo. When necessary, Zoric or Boris Cepin had contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And the other part of my question, sir, is who - at the end other, if you will - who were the persons, who were the officials at ODPR HVO, the Herceg-Bosna agency? Who were you dealing with there?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first person who we cooperated with was Mr. Tadic. After him, the second person, the head of the Office for Displaced Persons in Herceg-Bosna was Mr. Martin Raguz. I'm not sure when exactly he succeeded Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Tadic, that was Darinko Tadic, and I take it he was the head of ODPR HVO --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- prior to Mr. Rebic. You'll have to give a --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me ask you a somewhat different question, sir. You've mentioned a couple of occasions perhaps since you began testifying earlier this week, but can you tell the Judges approximately -- during the period, let's say from the middle of 1992, roughly July 1992, until mid-1994, perhaps we can say again July 1994, during that approximate two-year period how often did you go to, physically, Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Herceg-Bosna was not within my remit in any way, it was very rarely, I think maybe only once or, if my memory serves me well, twice, that I visited that office in Herceg-Bosna. There was no need for our office or members of our office to go there, because they were quite independent in their activities. They were not our extended arm, so there was no reason for us to go there, because we had no competence over that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you if you can be provided -- this will be in one of the Defence binders I believe you were shown the document by Mr. Karnavas, we may need the assistance of the usher, if you can please look at Exhibit 1D 02008. I'm told -- I don't know this, but I'm told by my very good colleague that that could be number 12 in the binder, one of the binders that people have been using. Do you have it, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll have it for you in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll get it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that we saw previously, that you looked at the other day. According to the information that we were provided, Dr. Rebic, this is a document that you're familiar with. You had indicated that Dr. Granic, who you identified as your boss, he informed you about this document and talked to you about it. There had been a meeting between Mr. Granic and Mr. Prlic because Mr. Granic indeed wanted to define the relations between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, and Dr. Granic and Dr. Prlic agreed that the Croatian ODPR would cooperate with establishing a similar office in Herceg-Bosna and to essentially, if you will, set that office up and get it running. That's what we've been told. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. At that time we didn't have time, Granic and I, that is, to discuss in detail all the aspects of the conclusions he had reached with other officials, but I was informed of this in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's several aspects of this document we will come back to because there's -- hopefully we'll approach our questions and answers in a topical way, and there are some things that I will come back to when it's perhaps more appropriate further into the examination, but on the current point, if I could ask you -- if I could direct your attention, for example, to paragraph number 2, paragraph number 5. You can just cast your eyes on those. This is consistent, is it not, with what you told us just a few moments ago that there would be efforts, ongoing efforts, between the ODPR Croatia and ODPR HVO to get the latter established and running and that there would be close coordination, cooperation, between those two agencies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not just that, Mr. Scott. It was necessary to organise on the territory of Herceg-Bosna accommodation for displaced persons within that area. That was what the Republic of Croatia had requested. It was not necessary for everyone to cross over into Croatia. Sarajevo and Mostar both, and this was one of the conclusions of the friendship agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic, it was necessary for both the Bosniak Muslim side and the Croatian side in cooperation with Croatia to take measures themselves to look after their displaced persons, and we would help them where they were unable to do this on their own if they were overwhelmed by the numbers of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. If you'd look at point number 7. Perhaps you can help us with this since you were the head of the agency in Croatia and working closely with Mr. Granic. Perhaps you can assist us. Point 7 says: "When contacting the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, ensure centralised access. The contact should be made only at the HVO HZ HB level, in other words, through an office set up by the HVO." Now, why in your experience, drawing on your experience as head of the ODPR Croatia, why would you want access centralised and limited only at a senior level?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand point 7, the Croatian side insisted that in Herceg-Bosna also conditions should be put in place assisted by the High Commissioner for Refugees, and Croatia would also assist in that respect. The ODPR was in daily contact with the High Commissioner, with the UNHCR, and there was some information, because I think the UNHCR did not have its own office in Mostar, so some contacts between the UNHCR and them went through us, but these contacts were not so numerous. Sometimes the UNHCR got involved in solving the problems of the ODPR in Mostar directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, perhaps we'll come to some of those instances. If I can just ask you to look briefly at one other part of the document before we finish with this document, at least for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then, perhaps, Your Honour, it might be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look at point 11, same document. If you can look at point 11, just in passing, so perhaps we don't have to come back to the document, at least in this respect. Another thing that Dr. Granic and Dr. Prlic apparently discussed at this meeting was the assistance of Croatia in operating the Mostar university; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The Republic of Croatia gave logistical assistance for the founding of Mostar university so that both Croats and Bosniaks in Mostar could become independent in this respect also rather than arriving in Zagreb or Sarajevo so that they could have and university in their own town, and that university still exists to this day, and our professors from Zagreb, especially from the medical school, still go to teach in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be a good time for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution has the floor again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, just on the topic of one of the accused in this case, Mr. Prlic, if you could just confirm my understanding, and again this is based on what I -- the information I've been given, if I can just confirm that with you for purposes of the record, you believe that you -- that Dr. Prlic visited Dr. Granic about a month before the fighting began in the Posavina, sometime after the war started with the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when I first met Mr. Prlic in Mr. Granic 's office. Mr. Granic was then the deputy prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist us, please, with any other -- I know it's some time ago, but if you can, can you give us any further information about the approximate date of that, your first meeting with Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the date. It might have been in the summer of 1992, maybe even a bit later in the autumn, towards the autumn. It was not an official meeting between me and Mr. Prlic. I happened to be in Mr. Granic's office. I had come to see the deputy prime minister about something we needed. I can't remember what. And in the break I met Mr. Prlic and had a brief conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me, in the interests of time, let me just indicate that again the information that I've been given is that during the time -- if we can say before or during the war, I'm not talking about -- I'm not talking about 1995 or anytime after that, but before and during the war you can recall meeting Dr. Prlic twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I'm certain about. Whether it was twice I can't be absolutely sure. I did attend some meetings which were held between representatives of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and Prlic was there, but he was in a crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And just to finish on this, again I understand that you do not recall having any what might be described as substantive conversations or communications with Dr. Prlic during the war, which again for these purposes we'll say 1992 to 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a conversation by telephone with Mr. Prlic. That I know. That was when there were about a hundred and fifty Bosnian Herzegovinian Muslims in the Zagreb mosque. On that occasion Mr. Mouchet called me up. He was very sad. He said, Professor, why are you no longer receiving Muslims? I said to Mr. Mouchet, this is the first I've heard of it, because we are receiving everyone who comes every day regardless of whether they are Bosnian Muslims or Bosnian Croats. He said to me that there were -- well, he said there were 800 of them in the mosque. There weren't that many, actually, as far as I can recall, and then I sent Mrs. Bozena Les who was then the head of the regional office to go to the mosque urgently and take a look and inform me of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would insist on the gentleman being allowed to complete his answer. It is part of the question that was being asked of him, and so I think he's entitled to give a full answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I'm entitled to a responsive answer and that is the conversation with Mr. Prlic. If the Chamber wants to give me more time then I'll be happy to do that, but my time is very limited. My question was very specific. I don't need the whole story. I want to know about his dealings. He mentioned he volunteered a phone conversation with Mr. Prlic concerning 150 Bosnian Muslims at the Zagreb mosque and I want to go straight to -- we understand that. I let the witness go on, but let's go straight now to the conversation with Mr. Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, Witness. You said you had a conversation with Mr. Prlic in this regard. Can you tell us what the nature of your conversation was with Mr. Prlic in connection with these Muslims being at the Zagreb mosque?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When together with Mr. Mouchet I went to the mosque and saw those people there, I asked them what they wanted. I asked them whether they wanted to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina or whether they wanted to ask for refugee status. They were in two minds. Mouchet advised me to receive them all and give them all refugee status, which is what we did. Then I called up Mr. Prlic, told him what had happened. I told him about a hundred and fifty refugees had arrived from Bosnia-Herzegovina and that we had not been previously informed, so they had to spend three days in the mosque, and they had not even applied to us, but it was only after the UNHCR intervened. Then Mr. Prlic said that he would examine the case and let me know. He called me back soon after that. He told me that he had investigated the case. He hadn't known anything about it previously, and that these were people who wanted to leave and go to Croatia to be somewhere safe. They were all people who had left the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian army in Herceg-Bosna. He said to me that they had paid for their transport and left because they felt they would be safer, their lives would be safer in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my contact with him. That's what it amounted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on that occasion, sir, and this actually goes back to what we were talking about before the break, and I asked you about your dealings with the ODPR HVO, the head of that agency I believe -- I believe around this time would have been Darinko Tadic. Why did you call Mr. Prlic? What caused you to think that Mr. Prlic was the person that you should contact to deal with this matter?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought he would provide me with the best information, better than the ODPR, and also we didn't communicate by telephone very often with that ODPR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me -- let me go further on that. You say you thought he would provide you with the best information. Why? Why did you think that? Why did you think that it would be Mr. Prlic that would provide you with the best information in this situation?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, firstly because I had already met him personally, so I knew him. And secondly, because he was a high-ranking HVO official. Therefore, he was a person who could give me the best information about those people. I wanted to know what sort of people they were and how they had left Bosnia-Herzegovina. His first reply was that he didn't know anything about it but that he would investigate. After he had investigated he called me up again and he told me what I just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I just want to clarify a couple of dates with you if we can. You mentioned in the course of your testimony that I think between 1992 -- well, no. I believe between 1993 and 1994 there were three times when there was a survey or a census of the persons who had come to Croatia from other countries during the war. We can use -- we can use the term "refugee" or "displaced person" generally, not necessarily in a technical sense but people who had moved, travelled to Croatia during that time, and you indicated at one point that the first census was in April, May, and June of 1992, and can I suggest to you, sir, that that would have been -- that would have been the second census in 1993, not in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I said. In 1992, that was the first census, and it concerned displaced persons in Croatia. In 1993 there was the second census -- or, rather, it was the first census of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the third census concerned both displaced persons and refugees and it took place in 1994. If I'm correct, it was sometime in June or July. So there were three censuses in all, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there was a census in February 1993. Isn't at that correct? And in fact, wasn't that the first census? That was the first census, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. No, no. In -- there was a later one in February. The first one in 1992 was in April and May and it ended in June. I'm using the Croatian language. I'm not looking at the transcript to see what the interpreter said. It was April, May, and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So April, June, 1992 was the first survey -- or census. Then in February 1993 was the second?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At about the same time, yes. The same months that is. A little later. I think it was completed in June, because the logistics were better, and the people knew better how to do it. It was done faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, the document, sir, the documentation and Dr. Zoric who testified here said that that survey took place in February of 1993. February. So might you be mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. You can check it in the documents. It's easy to check. I don't think I'm wrong. In 1993 there couldn't have been a census in February. In 1993, the census could have been taken in April, May, and June, the same months as the first one more or less. February, I think, is a little too early as far as I can recall. However, it can be checked in the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving to another date that I would just like to correct if we can, or clarify. You also mentioned in your testimony on Monday a meeting with, I think, Azra Krajsek and Mr. Tadic and perhaps Mr. Raguz as well, said there was a meeting to sit down and discuss a number of things and you said that meeting had taken place on the 11th of April, 1993. Can I suggest to you -- would you recall that in fact that meeting -- if you think about that particular meeting, that actually was in April 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I said, unless there was some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps it was -- perhaps it was some of our confusion. That's why I needed to ask and clarify.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So it might have been a misinterpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. April 1994. All right. Thank you for that. Let me ask you about some relationships with Franjo Tudjman since you were asked some questions about him. Again if I can focus your attention primarily on the period -- well, for this -- for this purpose 1991, 1994. Can you tell the Judges, please, how many times do you think you had any sort of face-to-face dealings, conversations, meetings with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as often as one might expect, because with reference to the refugee and displaced person situation, the president of the Republic of Croatia received direct briefings from Dr. Granic, who was my superior. However, I attended a meeting, for example, between representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia when relations between the two countries were being discussed and when the friendship agreement was signed. I shook hands with Tudjman on that occasion. Once I went to see the president together with the community of displaced persons from Croatia who were having certain problems regarding accommodation, food, and so on. These were Croatian citizens. And then the president invited me to attend the meeting, to hear their complaints and comment on them. That was a meeting when I was there in an official capacity, and before that I had a face-to-face meeting with the president and I told him that he should know that these were persons who could not be completely objective in their reports on their accommodation and food because they were stressed out, and he told me he knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, again, sir, I need to have -- I need to move forward, and I apologise for that, but again, as everyone knows, our time is limited, and you've already told us about your engagement this weekend which we would like to, of course, accommodate you. So so far you've told us about two meetings. So during 1991 to 1994, you had two meetings with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others. I was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, how many? I just -- please answer my question. I'm going to become increasingly -- I'm going to interrupt you because I don't need all your belong answers all the time, with my apology. My question is how many. You don't need to describe them. Do you understand? Two, four, ten? How many times did you meet with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, face-to-face only with once -- or twice. Excuse me, twice. Once with reference to refugees and their accommodation, and secondly when I resigned and he asked me to come and see him to try to -- and he tried to persuade me to remain at the head of the ODPR, and I told him no, I was definitely resigning. If you have questions about these two meetings, I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever during this 1991 to 1994 time period meet with Mr. Susak, the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Not face-to-face, but together with other persons in connection with accommodating and securing displaced persons. Once I went to see him with the minister of health, Dr. Hebrang, and Dr. Kostovic, the Deputy Prime Minister, and Doctor -- what was his name? He was a Doctor too. I can't recall his last name right now. That was just before Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So let me ask you, sir, how many times, how many times, a number -- what I'm asking you for is a number. How many times did you --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, we're talking face-to-face, four eyes, four ears. That's what the gentleman is talking about, so we don't have confusion about how many times he was in the room where discussions were being help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that we're clear on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not talking about just one-on-one meetings where it was just and Mr. Tudjman or you and Mr. Susak, but times when you had face-to-face dealings, there may have been other people in the meeting. So so far you've had two with President Tudjman and one with Dr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's incorrect. Again he's using "face-to-face meetings," and I'm saying that the way you -- you're shaking your head, Judge Trechsel, but hear me out, please. When the gentleman is saying face-to-face, he's talking one to one, nobody else in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
