utterances.text: How does Mr. Karnavas know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do know that. Because I do know that. Now -- now -- now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Michael, Michael.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Part of it has to do with the language. Now, the question needs to be rephrased. When he's talking about face-to-face, that's what's throwing the gentleman off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Michael. Michael. I'm going to make a genuine attempt to calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise, but you don't need to calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Michael --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We need precision in the courtroom, and the gentleman is entitled to have precise questions. I appreciate your candour and you want to help, but the issue here is: In his own language what does face-to-face mean, and it's interpreted differently in Croatian than it is, say, in English. So he's talking about meetings. I think we need to make a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, don't start on me. Ms. Alaburic and I discussed exactly this point. This is precisely what we were trying to help with. Ms. Alaburic has explained to me what the witness has been saying in his own language. There is a very simple but repeated and understandable issue which comes up in the interpretation which is that face-to-face in English is less apt than the phrase one to one or one on one. Face-to-face in English doesn't just mean just two people together, it means as opposed to on the telephone, for example. It means physically present. Probably, and I'm as complimentary as anybody about the interpretation here, but probably whatever phrase the witness is using in his own language, as explained by my learned leading counsel, is better translated as one-to-one rather than face-to-face and that would avoid the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is obviously a semantical problem. Mr. Stewart thinks it's better to say one to one while the interpreters were saying face-to-face. And Mr. Scott, please try to perhaps be a little bit more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just for the clarity, if you look at page 45, line 6, the witness in answering the question of the Prosecutor, which was to the meetings said, "I did meet Mr. Susak not face-to-face but together with other persons." So he gave a clear answer, I think. And then the question was whether this was more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. That's what alerted us to the fact that there was clearly this confusion which we've tried to help clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, it's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the issue goes to President Tudjman as well, and you have to look at page 43, 44, and then if you look at the way the question is being phrased, and there's no ill-intention on the part of the Prosecution. However, something is being lost in translation. And I understand the line of questioning. In other words, you haven't met him therefore you can't opine on what the gentleman was thinking. That's the line of questioning, but I think we need to be fair because the gentleman indicated that he was present in the room. So the follow-up question might be, Well, how often were you present in the room where things were being discussed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French language may perhaps come to the rescue and solve this issue. In French the right way of putting the question would be, "When did you see personally Mr. Tudjman or Mr. Susak or individually," and the word individually or personally means that there were only two persons present. So in other words it goes back to what Mr. Stewart was saying, one to one. But the French language is a very precise language. So, Mr. Scott, please put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just for the record I'm not excited about any of this. If there has been in fact -- if there is a cultural or translation issue, then I appreciate being alerted to it, but I have to agree with Judge Trechsel. I heard the same thing and it seemed to me, listening to witness's answer, that he perfectly understood - it appeared to me - what was translated and what came on the screen, that he perfectly well understood, so I had no reason to think otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me, Witness, we'll have to take this a bit longer, which is fine, I suppose, as long as the Chamber allows us to move in this way. I'm not limiting my question to you in terms of one to one, and that's not my understanding. You know a one to one meeting is if you and I were in the room somewhere and it was just the two of us. Nobody else. That's not what I'm talking, you understand. That's not what I'm talking about. But I'm talking about times where you were in a meeting, it could be just the two of you, but it also could be -- Susak could have been there, Sarinic could have been there, anybody could have been, and I want you to tell us how many times between 1991 and 1994 were you physically present with President Tudjman in that sort of a way. And I don't mean in a conference hall with 5.000 people, but in a meeting, personal dealings, direct dealings with him that way. Now, I hope -- you're an extremely well-educated man, you speak a number of languages including English, so I hope you understand what I mean. Can you assist us? Does that change your answer? Was it those two times or is it -- would you like to add or change, modify your answer?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat and this may assist you. I met Mr. President Tudjman only twice, face-to-face, individually, tete-a-tete. There were other meetings, for example a meeting between the two parties when the agreement on friendship was discussed. There may have been maybe five such meetings that I attended. As for Susak, I never met him face-to-face or individually or tete-a-tete. There was always another person or two more persons present who were dealing with some topical issues at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, the answer is no -- as you say, no individual meetings, no personal meetings with Mr. Susak. Going back to President Tudjman, then, so hopefully we can move forward, have you now indicated then, based on everything you've heard in the courtroom over the last 15 minutes, that during this time period you may have had five physical interventions, if you will, occasions to be with President Tudjman between 1991 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were such occasions, but as I sit here today, I can't recall them all. One of them was definitely the friendship meeting that I mentioned and the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We know about that. We have a transcript of that meeting. Sir, we have a transcript of that meeting. Everyone knows about that one.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other meetings were the one when he was at the session of the government of the Republic of Croatia. I was there, and that was in 1995. I was there together with other persons. I was also with him when I was decorated. Again there were other people present. And I really can't recall any other particular occasions when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll move forward sir. Now, you're familiar, are you not, there was a body in the Croatian government or at the time, and maybe there still is, something called the Council for Defence and National Security, I understand sometimes called the VONS for short, abbreviation. Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: VOS. I never attended VOS meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you for correcting me if I was wrong. That's not the information that I was provided. But in any event you've seen -- you've gone straight to my question, sir. Thank you. You never attended any of those meetings. And so the Judges know, that was an extreme important body that was primarily involved in the -- setting the defence and national security strategy for Croatia during that time period; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but I as the head of the of ODPR was not requested as a member of that body or at its meetings. It was just not necessary for me to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said on Monday, sir, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, but in order to avoid any future confusion, the abbreviation VOS stands for military and security intelligence service, and what the Prosecutor is talking about is actually VONS which is the council for defence and national security, whereas VOS is the intelligence military service.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. You're right there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Praljak. We can agree on that. I was right the first time. It was the VONS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So moving forward then, and we know that you did not attend any of the meetings of that body. Now, when you testified on Monday, you said that Tudjman busied himself with the idea of reviving the old agreement between the Serbs and Croats. Now, when you say he busied himself, what did you mean to say by that? How do -- number one, how do you know, and number two, assuming you do know something about it, what do you mean he busied himself with the idea of reviving the old agreement?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, when I said he was dealing with the idea of Banovina Croatia, I primarily referred to him as the candidate of the HDZ and as a politician, and at the same time as a historian, as a person who was quite familiar with not only the history of Croatia after the Second World War but also the history before the war, and he was familiar with the agreement between Serbs and Croats dating back to 1939 dealing with the autonomy of Croatia. This autonomy also comprised parts of the current territory of today's Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As the political candidate, in his speeches I remember that as a citizen who listened to those speeches, he would he occasionally mention that idea and he would say that this Banovina of Croatia could be re-established. However, from the moment when Bosnia-Herzegovina was seceded from Yugoslavia and became an independent state, and Croatia was the first to recognise it as an independent state, and Croatia was also among the first states that established diplomatic contacts with the newly created state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as of that moment on Tudjman stopped insisting [as interpreted] on the re-establishment of Banovina, because at the moment when Bosnia-Herzegovina was established as an independent state within the borders of the former Republic of Yugoslavia, the issue of Banovina for him became moot and history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's a clarification. I'm told that the gentleman did not say that Tudjman stopped insisting, that he never insisted. And so I would ask that the gentleman be -- look at the screen and be given an opportunity to correct the record. Page 52, line 12. It says that, "At that moment Tudjman stopped insisting." He's saying that he never insisted. This is what my colleague tells me, who is a B/C/S speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you spent the last few minutes telling us that indeed, you confirmed for us, that as a politician, as an HDZ politician, Tudjman did speak about re-establishing the 1939 Banovina. So apparently he did talk about it at some point. So did he stop -- did he stop at some point pushing that idea and, if so, when and how do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm going to object to the form of the question. He never said he pushed the idea. It's one thing as a politician to express ideas. This is why I'm going to be on my feet and I'm going to be extremely aggressive at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you speak many languages, starting with your mother tongue, and you're perfectly able to express yourself in that language, but you also speak English. Can you please tell us again what happened with Tudjman and the Banovina? You see that it's a very important matter here and that tensions are ripe when we deal with this matter, so can you repeat what your feeling was in terms of Tudjman and the Banovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said and I will repeat, as a citizen who was listening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down for the interpreters to properly translate what you have to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a citizen I was listening to the candidate of the Croatian Democratic Union running for elections in 1990, and I heard him mentioning the fact of Banovina Croatia, which was established in 1939. When the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, when it was recognised by Croatia, which also included him, when diplomatic relations were established with the state, i.e., the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after that I did not hear him insisting on this idea. On the contrary, he had recognised the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the borders that it had before, and as of that time on this issue for him was history. I personally never discussed the issue with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in French we have a word, the word "insist," and I see that in English, in the English transcript, the word "insisting" has been used. In your own language did you use that word? Did you use the word "insist," or did you use another word, because from a linguistic point of view if you use the word "insist" it implies that you mentioned the issue in the past but at some point you stop dealing with it. So I'd like to know whether it's indeed the word "insist" that you used in your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No longer insisted, which means that he no longer pondered upon the idea of re-establishing Banovina Croatia. I repeat, he was totally clear on the fact that by having recognised the new state of Republic of Croatia -- of Bosnia, he as a politician, he could only talk about something that used to exist but no longer existed, nor did he want the idea to come to fruition, because that possibility no longer existed. That happened once he recognised the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a newly independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you just said a moment ago that you never personally discussed it with him, and when you say he no longer insisted, what you're telling the Chamber is you no longer heard him say it publicly, and he didn't say it to you. Now, that's what you're really telling us; right? He wasn't saying it publicly, and he didn't say it to you personally. That's all you can really tell us; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that he never personally spoke about that to me, and I did not hear him speak about that in public after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward then, sir, I've seen somewhere where you've expressed the view that you -- perhaps you and other people in Croatia at the time thought that the Serbs or the JNA were using refugees and displaced persons essentially as a weapon against Croatia, that is by flooding Croatia with refugees it would be a burden on the Croatian government and economy. Is that correct? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood me well, and this indeed is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to go to, please, Exhibit 1D 02277. It should be next to you I'm told. 1 -- 1D 2277. This is a document that I believe Mr. Karnavas showed to you. It is a letter from a group of refugees --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a number of binders here. We have your own binder. We have exhibits, other exhibits that are loose, and we have another binder, a blue binder. So can you specify what binder we're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll try to help as much as I can, Your Honour. The problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be in one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The blue one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It should be the number one from ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we refer to a Defence exhibit, it will, perhaps with very limited exceptions, be in the Defence binder. Obviously we didn't want to copy it yet another time, but we do understand the burden on everyone in the courtroom with juggling these materials. I think perhaps most people have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you can look at that document which again Mr. Karnavas showed you a letter dated the 7th of March, 1994 to Jadranko Prlic. Just a couple of brief questions hopefully. You've had extensive dealings with the -- with refugee issues and displaced persons issues, and you've told us in the last few days that these people -- it's a very unhappy situation for everyone. They often have complaints. I suppose who wouldn't? But in the middle -- approximately the middle of this letter, and I don't know if the paragraphs are the same in the Croatian language it would be about -- if I can ask you to look at the fifth paragraph that starts with the words "One school year." If you see that. I'll give you that --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Skipping -- we'll come back to something else in a moment, but skipping towards the end of that paragraph, you talk about such -- oh excuse me. I'm sorry. The letter talks about such things as insecurity, frustration, anxiety, various neuroses, trauma, shock. I mean, you would agree would you not these are serious matters or not, or are they frivolous?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are. You're correct there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that would be true no matter if the refugee is a Croat or a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going back earlier in the paragraph, you mention -- I apologise. I don't want to keep doing that. The letter mentions a school year being lost because the children were not able to attend classes "in their mother tongue," bracket, end bracket. Now, I'm sure you touched on this during your earlier examinations. Can you assist the Judges further? I mean, how much of a distinction was there at that time in 1993, 1994, between the Croatian language, what -- the language that Croats spoke and the language that the Bosniaks spoke? As I understand it, correct me if I'm wrong, but as I understand it they could understand and communicate perfectly well with each other, for the most part. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. They could perfectly understand each other. In Bosnia-Herzegovina the language spoken there is predominantly Croatian. Actually, the language -- the Croatian language spoken in Herzegovina is what we base our standard Croatian variant on. When I arrived as a student in grammar school, I didn't understand my teachers, but when it comes to the differences between Croats and Muslims, they understand each other perfectly, but let me clarify. Both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Croatian -- in Croatia Croats have a variant of Croatian which we called "received pronunciation," which is somewhat different from the Bosniak language which, during the times of the former Yugoslavia, was under the influence of the Serb language. Now, when it comes to a situation where people are under a lot of stress, even one Serbian word would not go down well with them. It would not have the same effect on me or my friends, but these are people who were under a lot of stress and even a single word could have annoyed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you that then, and that's -- it would be interesting to have a much longer linguistic discussion if we had the time, but I asked you earlier about these other concerns that were later -- expressed later in the paragraph, frustration, anxiety, but can you tell the Judges, how -- was that a serious issue that these people were not receiving -- children were not receiving classes in their mother tongue (Croatian). Was that a serious issue or really it's trivial?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. How can this gentleman opine on whether it was serious to those individuals or not? It might be serious to Dr. Rebic, it may not. You know, it all depends on the individuals and the circumstances. I don't believe that this gentleman is competent to answer that question. I think it's -- it's improperly phrased and it's unfair to ask a question of that dimension.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In your dealings with refugees or groups of refugees during the time 1992 to 1994, is this sort of things -- is this something you heard only once or did you hear it on a number of occasions, that is, complaints about not being able to use one's own language? Or is this a one time -- kind of a one-time situation?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to be able to understand the text. The lost year here and the education in the Bosniak language refers to their stay in Central Bosnia, probably in Vares or in Kakanj, under the Muslim control. When they arrived in Pineta, they had education in their own Croatian language, the language that they had been brought up on in Central Bosnia, Posavina, and Herzegovina. Even to this day Croats can follow Croatian television, newspaper, and they speak is the so-called Croatian proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir, and it's like with English. There are various dialects, I suppose, and accents of English. I'm sure Mr. Stewart thinks that I speak English terribly, but in any event, let me just -- my point is this: The point is these children went to school -- apparently they went to classes. The classes used a language that they -- is perfectly well understood. So what difference did it make that it was not in "Croatian"? Was this just a made-up issue?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One has to read what these people say in the text. They say a year was lost because they were -- it was intentionally made impossible for them to attend classes in their mother tongue, Croatian. The Muslims in Kakanj or Vares were asking of these children who spoke the pure Croatian language at home to suddenly have imposed on them a language which we in Croatia and the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina that had for a long time considered to represent Serbisation of the Croatian language, which got on our nerves both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia. And it still does, because they used to talk about the Serbo-Croatian language which does not exist. There is the Serbian language and the Croatian language. In Bosnia-Herzegovina there are areas which are more under the influence the Serbian language and other areas which are more under the influence of the Croatian language and that's where the Croatians and the Muslims mostly live.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's move forward, and for better or worse I think that's as much time we can spend on that topic unless the Judges have questions. Sir, you've mentioned I think perhaps more than once in the course of your testimony that the Croatian border, that is the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, was never closed to Muslims during the -- during the war, and again let's say 1992, 1994. But you've also -- let me just tell you, sir, you've also indicated on a number of occasions that various paperwork, transit visa, permits, approval, permission, some sort of documentation was required or the border police or what have you would not allow people to come across the border. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are correct. It's correct that when the refugees were crossing the official border crossings between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia they had to have documents. If they took other routes where there was no control of the border, and they did, then they would arrive without being stopped by anyone and find themselves in Zagreb, and somebody would call me up and say, "Hey, wait a minute."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. All right. We all understand that in every country people can enter illegal little not going through regulated check-points but if a person were to enter Croatia during this period legally through an established custom point or what he would call it, an immigration point, they would require some sort of paperwork to cross the border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I would say -- well, I would not say they would have to have paperwork but that they should have had paperwork, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Just a couple of other questions. I'm just trying to touch on a few things before we move into some specific topics. Mr. Karnavas, I believe, showed you document -- I don't think you necessarily need to look at it. If you want to I certainly won't prevent you, but it was 1D 02634, which was a document about the steering committee of the ODPR for Croatia, and I just -- my question to you about that, sir, is it correct, that, at least as far as I could tell, there was -- was there any Muslim member on that steering committee or were there any Islamic charities or humanitarian organisations who were represented on the steering committee?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that committee, Mr. Scott, there was no one of the Muslim faith, because in Croatia there is not a significant number of Muslims. I think they amount to 1 or 1.5 per cent of the population. But there were very good relations between the ODPR and Merhamet in Zagreb, and there were frequent meetings between Aganovic, who was the head of that Merhamet office, or was legally responsible for that office. We met very often both in Merhamet and in my own office, especially in relation to humanitarian convoys and humanitarian aid for Muslims. We were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with the financing of these efforts, and let me say that no one -- well, I won't speak for everyone in the courtroom, of course, I don't question, I never have questioned, that the Republic of Croatia spent a great deal of money dealing with refugees and humanitarian issues, but just so the record is clear, based on the information again that I was provided in connection with your evidence, can you confirm for us for the purposes of the trial record that the establishment of the Croatian refugee centres, and by that I mean centres that were operated in the Republic of Croatia supported by the Croatian government, were paid approximately 80 per cent funded -- funded, if you will, 80 per cent by the Croatian government with the rest coming either from the UN or the -- well, what we would now call the EU; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Touching on Ms. Turkovic, she came up a number of times. Again, and my understanding, sir, is that you met with Ms. Turkovic on a number of occasions. She would come and visit your office or visit you in your office. You had good relations with her. When there were problems she raised them with you. She may have on occasion had problems with local centres when those centres did not follow your instructions. Is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall and provide to the Judges any information about instances where people in the local centres did not follow your instructions? Your instruction might be to do A, but the people out there on the ground, so to speak, were not doing what you told them to do. Can you give us some examples of that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An example of that, Mr. Scott, might be the revocation of refugee status, for example. Although instructions were sent out from the office to everyone, evidently not everyone read them through with the same care. There was an overall decision to revoke the status, but there were certain conditions under which the status would not be revoked but would, rather, be extended. I may not need to repeat this, but it concerned people's whose house had been destroyed, who were ill, who had children in school, or who lived in areas where there was still tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can paraphrase another witness that the Chamber will recall, is it fair to say, sir, that it's one thing to give directions and another thing to have them carried out.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, which is why we decided that these instructions had to be respected. And we had a meeting with Ms. Turkovic and Krajsek and Ms. Hratokovic [phoen] and Darinko Tadic and Martin Raguz, because when the status was revoked, Mr. Prlic also complained about this as did the Bosnian-Herzegovinian embassy. Everyone from his own standpoint, of course. Mr. Prlic was unable to receive large numbers of people who would be welfare cases, and evidently the Bosnian embassy had its reasons also. Their problem was where to -- where to receive the Muslims, where to accommodate them. So they were in a more sensitive situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you raised again Mr. Prlic. Now, is this the same -- is this the same one conversation you referred to earlier, or are you now telling us about another conversation with Dr. Prlic about refugees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it's not a conversation. It's a document, a letter sent by Mr. Prlic to the government of the Republic of Croatia and the prime minister, that is, and then the prime minister forwarded the letter to me for my information. He probably also copied it to the office. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Sir, in looking at your report, the document that we were provided which is 1D 02921, titled "My Work at the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees," just a couple of questions on that. You have an entry for the 13th of November, and I'll have to rely on everyone to proceed chronologically through the document, but if you can find your entry for the 13th of November, 1992. You make reference to travelling to Belgrade "for a secret meeting with representatives of Yugoslav authorities. President Granic was there and some other ministers." I wonder if you might tell us what that secret meeting was about.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a secret meeting that was never spoken about in the Croatian media. It was an attempt to solve some pressing issues which, as regards my office, the ODPR, were refugees, people expelled from their homes. There were others who were representing the economy or the educational system. There were several of us who tried in this way to mitigate the consequences of the aggression --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and to make some shifts --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. But why was it secret?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you about back to that time, it was war. There was aggression, and to speak in public about it would have caused an uproar both in Serbia and Croatia. It would have had bad consequences, and the meeting would not have been possible at all. That's why it was secret. If I recall, if I'm not wrong, the prime minister at the time was a gentleman who had arrived from America. Mr. Praljak will help me. What was his name? Tadic? Oh, yes, Panic, Panic. That's right, Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke and lot. He talked a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We know a lot of people like that. If I can still stay in your report, in early April -- my apology. In early February 1993, you refer to the registration of refugees. It says: "In early February 1993, together with UNHCR, we started registering all refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia." And I just wonder sir, that might refresh your recollection to the questions I put to you earlier this afternoon. Wasn't that census or survey in 1993 in February? It's in your report.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it says February, that's an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. The report is in error. So you still --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an error in the report, yes, because the census of 1993 was in the months of April, May, and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those three months. Such errors are always possible when reports are compiled, but we do have documents, precise documents on the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you say in your report: "UNHCR would cover the expenses of registering as had been the case with the Croatian displaced persons the year before. We had an excellent experience from that project." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can jump all the way to February of 1994, you have an entry which says for the 7th of February --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could we have page numbers? It's easier for us to kind of track.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 20. Page 20 at least in the English version. I'm sorry, that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But proceeding chronologically through the document, if you can go -- if you can find -- there's an entry, sir, in your report on the 7th of February 1994 and it says: "I went to see Professor Mate Granic. He advised me how to behave in Livno where I was going the following day to the all-Croatian Assembly of BiH Croats." First of all, do you recall what this meeting, this all-Croatian Assembly in Livno was in February 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a meeting of Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a meeting which did not have primarily political connotations but, rather, cultural connotations. It was a meeting of all Croats together to consider issues, and I can't recall in detail today what these issues were. I'm sure it had to do with independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, sir, you are again a highly educated man. Now -- you had now been in your post for some years. You certainly were very experienced in what you were doing. How is it that it was necessary for Mr. Granic to advise you how to behave at the meeting in Livno? What did he tell you? What instructions did he give you about attending and participating in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave me advice. He said if I was asked to speak at that meeting that I should speak on behalf of the ODPR in a way that would avoid any political implications following from my speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, February 1994 was right around the time of -- that the Washington Agreement was beginning to get some traction. It was signed later in March, I believe. Do you recall whether Mr. Granic gave you any particular instructions on what your position should be at that time in case the topic of the Washington Agreement came up at this meeting in Livno?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't understand your question very well. In connection with what, the Washington Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. Sorry if I wasn't clear. Around this time the Chamber has heard extensive evidence that around early 1994 there began to be discussions -- or continued to be discussions, lest there be any objection, about something that came to be known as the Washington Agreement, which I believe was signed in either late February or March of 1994. And I just wondered do you recall any of Dr. Granic's instructions to you touched upon the Washington Agreement, how that should be presented or what stance you should take about that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, moving to the specific questions about refugees in Croatia, which obviously we've talked a great deal about, we understand, sir, and there's already been evidence in the case that in -- on or about the 13th of July, 1992, there was a decision by the Croatian government or an announcement not to accept any more refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that essentially Croatia was, we might say, full. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, but that was more a cry for help to third countries rather than a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall how long that situation continued; that is, for how long did Croatia stop receiving additional refugees, and did the reception of refugees by Croatia then start again at some point and, if so, can you give us the dates?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia never stopped receiving refugees. It simply couldn't do that. What you say the government decided, I don't remember the decision in detail or with precision, but I would interpret it now more as an expression of distress, the distress in which the country found itself, and a possible stopping of taking in refugees, but in fact the reception of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina never stopped. We continued taking in refugees every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll come back to that in the course of the examination. Let me just ask more general questions about refugees and displaced persons. Would you agree, sir, that there was a difference -- other witnesses and evidence have told us that there was a difference between someone who had -- and I'm now talking in a very technical sense, refugee status, who had been given the legal status of refugee. That had significance as opposed to someone who did not have refugee status; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference between a person who had refugee status and a person who was not a refugee either because they were not a refugee de facto and didn't need the refugee status because they were well accommodated and didn't want to be socially branded as a refugee or perhaps simply did not wish to have that status for reasons of their own, that was the only difference, but everyone who did have the status of a refugee or displaced persons had all the rights they were entitled to, and they were all protected. May I explain that according to our censuses, about 6 per cent of the persons who had arrived from Bosnia-Herzegovina had not requested refugee status. These were intellectuals, people who were well off, people who had houses in Croatia, weekend cottages or villas by the sea. They didn't ask for those and there were about 6 per cent of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. But there was an entire legal system, if you will, sir, there were laws, statutes, legislation, there was a bureaucracy to deal with the granting of refugee status, and you either -- at one point in time you either had it -- you either had it under the law or you didn't have it. And if you had refugee status under the law, that gave rise to certain rights that you did not have if you did not have that legal status; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but the reason these people didn't have that status was that they simply didn't need to be assisted. They didn't need the kind of care that refugee status would provide them with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not talking -- I don't know exactly what you're referring to, but I'm not talking about this 6 per cent. I'm -- you're saying that the only people -- are you telling the Chamber that the only people who didn't get refugee status in Croatia, the only people who didn't get it are the ones who didn't ask for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what he stated, and I suggest that perhaps Mr. Scott go back and rephrase his questions, because I think now we're getting into some murky areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe what Mr. Scott wishes to get from the witness is the benefits that one enjoyed being a refugee versus somebody who was not a refugee or was not a declared refugee, what sort of benefits or lack thereof. I think that's what he's trying to get at. So perhaps he could rephrase the questions, but I think now he's putting words into the witness's mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please try to reformulate the question since it seems to raise a problem. I do not share that point of view. If there's a problem, let's try to solve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nor do I, Your Honour, so I won't use my time to pursue it further. The witness seems to understand, and I think everyone in the courtroom has understood perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me move on to a specific law. If I can ask you to look, please, at 1D 02588. It will be in one of the Defence binders. First binder I'm told. Actually, we're probably all spending more time finding the document than we really need, but just so everyone knows what we're talking about, that is decree dated the 27th of October, 1992, which Mr. Karnavas showed you, I believe, and you've indicated, I believe, that this -- you consider this to be the law that your agency was applying, following, in connection with displaced persons and refugees; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that is your understanding despite the fact that the decree on its face only applies to internally displaced persons in Croatia and says nothing about persons coming from outside Croatia? You agree that that's what the Statute says on its face? It says nothing about people coming from outside.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find an article that would directly mention refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, the definition of a refugee implies everybody who was expelled from Bosnia and Herzegovina and arrived in Croatia. This decree provided a definition that a refugee is the person who had been expelled from a neighbouring state and arrived in Croatia, and the neighbouring state could have been Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Vojvodina, or Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for -- I'd rather not have to cut you off. I'm not trying to be rude, but you say that, sir, but you're saying that's your interpretation, but that's not what the law says. That's not -- there's no language, I'll represent to you -- everyone in the courtroom can read it ten times. That's not what the statute says -- the decree says. Now, let me ask you to go next to 1D 02368 -- excuse me my apology, 1D 02638. It's either, I'm told, in the second or third binder. And once again I'm not really going to go through the details of the statute or the decision or the law, but this is a law on the status of displaced persons and refugees which we understand went into effect sometime around the 18th of October, 1993, and we can see on the page or in the document, and it's my understanding, sir, that it's your position or it's the position of the ODPR Croatia that this again -- when this law went into effect that this was the law that your agency followed and applied in connection with displaced persons and refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, but we in the office, in keeping with the 1951 Geneva Conventions, regarded as refugees all those persons who arrived from a different state of the former Yugoslavia in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. If this is not contained in the law, and I didn't have the time to study it, this was still the practice of our office and the practice was clear. We followed that practice -- practice in our work, and this was the practice that the government had to adopt in adopting my reports, and my reports contained the clear definitions of displaced person as a person who was displaced from their place of origin in Croatia, and refugee was a person who arrived from Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were expelled from there and was received by the Republic of Croatia. That's why we made this distinction and nobody ever objected to any of my reports saying that I was doing something contrary to the decision or to the law for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm not being critical of you. Please don't -- please don't misunderstand. I'm not being critical of what you did. I'm just trying to --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely understand I'm just trying to clarify things and tell you how we worked, in any case you know that legislation is never perfect, and especially when it's applied in war situations when we had other things on our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. But the point -- the only point for now, and I want just to confirm that is the law in fact that you considered to apply, but once again, and I think that everyone in the courtroom has already seen that we've gone over this with another -- at least one other witness. The statute on its face, the words of the law are only limited to persons within the Republic of Croatia or people from Croatia who did flee abroad but from the Republic of Croatia, and it says nothing about people coming into the Republic of Croatia as refugees from outside the country. So there again -- what you've told us there's an interpretation that was put on the statute according to you but even though that's not what the statute says on its face; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I be even more specific? I worked with people, not with papers. I worked with people under certain circumstances and in certain situations, and those situations were such that people were either displaced within Croatia or had been refugees from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Through my contacts with UNHCR, through my own work, I can tell you that we had -- we established a practice that was quite clear and that reflected in all of our documents and in all of our reports. If the law was different, then I was governed by humanitarianism, bearing in mind that I was dealing with people rather than with papers, laws, and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could ask you to turn next to 4D 01232, which is the -- I think it's a document that Ms. Alaburic has shown to you. It's the law on the movement and residence of foreigners. 4D 01232. And -- I understand that there is a loose hard copy of this document because there's been at least a partial translation of the various -- some the various relevant articles. Sir, this is a law which you've seen before, shown to you and discussed previously, but this is indeed a law that appears on its face to, in fact, apply to refugees coming from outside the Republic of Croatia, and yet if I understand correctly you're saying you did not consider this law applied; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what we have here is we have two laws, the 1992 law and the 1993 law, who don't apply on their face but you say apply. And then we have another law, the law on foreigners, who does apply on its face but you say it doesn't apply. Now why -- can you tell us, can you help the Judges why that is the case? What explains this situation? Why doesn't the law on foreigners apply? By its terms it would appear to.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that once Yugoslavia disappeared a new situation was put in place. When Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbia became independent states, new circumstances arose for our Ministry of the Interior, and they had to adopt a certain behaviour towards foreigners who arrived from different countries, Slovenia, Hungary, Germany, to mention but a few. It is my impression that this is a decision that applied to those citizens. On the other hand, there was a separate law that applied to the movement of refugees, because refugees could not have been encompassed within a law --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. We have the law, for example, the second law, the law from 1993, and you've told us for some days now, and Dr. Zoric told us also for some days, that by -- by the middle of 1993 there was a huge refugee problem in Croatia, and clearly it must have been something considered by the Croatian parliament, and -- is the Chamber to believe that the legislators in Croatia didn't know how to write a law that would apply to people coming into Croatia from outside the country? They made exactly the same mistake not once but twice in writing legislation to deal with this issue?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question, because at the time I did not deal with these documents. The ODPR dealt with looking after refugees and displaced persons rather than with documents about the movement of foreigners. In any case, in our office for refugees and displaced persons we had a legal department as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, precisely I was going to put this question to you since the status of refugees is a very complex legal issue. I was going to ask you the question if -- precisely this, if within your office you had somebody who was able to bring up the Geneva Conventions of 1951. Those conventions are very clear. Did somebody show you various texts of internal law that could be applied to foreigners and to refugees, and that service or that department or that person, were they able to bring you a legal expertise in order to help you to head this office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the ODPR there was a legal service or a legal department, and this legal service dealt with all those various documents. At the beginning of our work in the office we had joint meetings where we analysed things, particularly the Geneva Conventions and laws that concerned refugees and displaced persons. This was a time, and I'm particularly referring to the year 1992, when we actually learned on the job. We learned the definitions of displaced persons, refugees. There were many people in Zagreb who could not make a distinction. We learned on the job. We even invited a lawyer from UNHCR. I can't remember the gentleman's name. I believe it was either Heinemann or somebody else and this gentleman delivered a lecture on the Geneva Conventions and what it says about looking after refugees. In other words, we embarked on a learning process on how to deal with the issue. And once when we managed to muster the international law we passed the knowledge on to others, when we were able to fully apply these laws that the Republic of Croatia inherited from the former Yugoslavia and adopted all of them by text that we already saw earlier today. All these laws, particularly those that concerned DPs and refugees, could be found in our office and they were the foundation of our work. One thing is sure. Some things arose from the law and from the decree, and even more things arose from -- from our everyday, day-to-day contact with the real situation, with the problems that arose day in and day out. And this was another source of learning for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I'm being told by the registrar that we need to break. We'll break for 20 minutes. The Prosecutor has used one hour and 37 minutes so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you -- if you still have 4D -- the law on foreigners, 4D 01232 available to you. Do you still have it there?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have 233 though. Oh, yes, I do. 232. I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, just one final question on this. A final question on this topic before moving to some other exhibits, but let me ask you to go to Article 31 of the law on foreigners. I'm abbreviating that, but movement and residence of foreigners. If you go to Article 31, it says that, if you have that, it says: "A foreigner who has left the country whose citizen he is or in which he was permanently residing as a stateless person in order to avoid persecution for his political views or national origin, racial or religious affiliation, may be awarded the status after refugee." And based on discussions we've had over the past hour or so, sir, given that the status of the legislation in applying a law that doesn't apply on its face, that does not apply on its face, and not applying another law that appears to apply on its face, was there a studied effort by your agency and the Croatian government not to apply the law on foreigners because to do so would recognise that these people were religious, racial, or political persecuted persons?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this Article 31 in one way or another also applies to refugees that we worked with, although originally it applies to foreigners who were persecuted in their own countries for their political, racial, or religious affiliations. In our situation, however, when this comes to the ODPR, this law could have only been a framework law in a certain sense, but it was not a law on which our work could have been based, on which the recognition of the refugee status would be granted to persons who had fled from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, excuse me. Why? You say this was not a law on which our work could have been based." It's a law. It's a law in the Republic of Croatia adopted by, as far as we know -- duly adopted by the appropriate authorities, the Sabor or whoever, and it's a law. It's on the books. Your agency, your legal duty, your obligation is to enforce Croatian law. Now, when you say, "This was not law that we could enforce," why not? Or did your agency pick and choose which Croatian law to apply and those you wanted to apply and the ones you didn't want to apply?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may have been misunderstood. I said that this law was broader and that it concerned the movement and stay of foreigners in the Republic of Croatia, and that this law was applied by the Ministry of the Interior. It was enforced by them, and it was not in conflict with the law and the decree that the ODPR applied, and that office primarily received recognised refugee status and cared for refugees. In any case, this law was primarily applied by the Ministry of the Interior. It did not contradict what we were doing, but it was primarily applied by the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I know from experience where this is going. I know -- I know it primarily because Dr. Rebic is not a legal expert as we know from his CV, and I really don't know what is the foundation of the all the Prosecutor's questions, but what I'm saying is that we have wasted over 15 minutes after the Prosecution's question on page 72 when he first arrived at the decree on refugees, which is 1D 02638. In the first answer provided by the witness, which is on record on page 72, line 8, the witness started his answer in the following way, and I have to quote: "[In English] Correct. That we in the office in keeping with the 1951 Geneva Conventions regarding -- regarded as refugees all those persons who arrived from different state," et cetera, et cetera. And then the witness provided additional understanding of the law. And then the questions, answers, questions, answers. The Prosecution obviously disregard the fact that by this answer, maybe not put as a lawyer would do, but this sentence clearly shows for a person who is like in this, that it was implementation of international convention. Now, I can talk about qualified lawyer and knowing the domestic law. The Croatian constitution at that time before that time and today as many constitutions in Europe, and I understand in United States, also says that international conventions are obligatory. They should be implemented directly regardless of the domestic law. And the witness, not being lawyer, is having obviously some problem to explain us. But he did mention, and by the way, what is more important particularly having in mind the position of this witness, is de facto, not de jure because he's not a lawyer, de facto, and de facto situation he told us about cooperation with UNHCR, UNHCR sitting in his own office, UNHCR giving him advice so obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I get the point. I get the point. Witness, when Mr. Scott asked you an excellent question, I wondered if you understood the meaning of that question, and Mr. Kovacic realised the same thing. Mr. Scott also asked you a number of questions about the same things. You know without being a legal expert that there is a Geneva Convention of 1951, and the former Yugoslavia was a signatory. There are specific references to the Geneva Conventions in the Civil Code and the Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia. When Croatia became an independent state it adopted the entire corpus of international law and legislation. That's one thing. So first you have the domestic laws, the Croatian laws, including the law that Mr. Scott showed you. Article 1 of this law is extremely similar to what we find in the Geneva Convention from 1951. It is stated in that convention that someone may be granted refugee status if he is persecuted for political, racial reasons. And Mr. Scott is telling you quite rightly that this law applies to the office, to the ODPR. It applies to everyone in Croatia. That was the meaning of his question. And listening to all this I wondered if you had grasped the meaning of the question. Now that you've heard my explanation, do you get the meaning of the question that Mr. Scott put to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I'm not a lawyer, I understand what all of you are talking about, but this is precisely how I answered. I replied that the law on movement and residence of foreigners in the Republic of Croatia did not contradict what we were doing. On the contrary. The article that was quoted, and I believe it was Article 31, was practised in our office as well. But on top of that, our office abided by the Geneva Conventions on looking after refugees and recognising the refugee status for all the persons arriving from a neighbouring country. And I've already told you that that's why we learned about the Geneva Conventions, that we had seminars together with UNHCR, that we had a legal office in our office which was very familiar with all these laws and conventions, and when we had our joint meetings it was present to brief us about any legal problems that we might have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I believe I understand what you're saying. Not only did you apply the Geneva Conventions at the office, but you also stated that on top of that you took care of these people. If I understand correctly, not only did your office grant refugee status to a number of individuals, but your office also provided material, health-related assistance, to all these people who arrived in the country. Is that the way I should interpret your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how my answer should be understood. And let me just clarify. If these refugees had arrived in Pakistan, they were not within the purview of my office. They -- our office would not have been charged with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I understand what you are telling us. Mr. Scott, you have the floor. We've tried to shed some light on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm -- I'm finished with the topic. I think the record will speak for itself at this point. Just to respond very briefing to Mr. Kovacic. First off, I didn't show the witness a single document that wasn't shown to him by the Defence. I didn't raise it. I didn't -- these are all documents the Defence put to the witness, so I simply came back across on cross-examination to the same exhibits. We can all agree, of course, that Mr. -- Dr. Rebic is not a lawyer, but he's, again, a highly educated man who from 1991 to 1996 was the head of an agency whose very job was to apply Croatian law in reference -- and international law, and international law, to the subject of refugees and displaced persons. So I give him the benefit of the doubt that he knew -- knew that what -- what his job was and the laws that did apply, including all the laws on the books of Croatia, including the ones that applied on their face as opposed to the ones which didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, if I can direct your attention to P 10406. P 10406. And that should be in the Prosecution's exhibits, I believe. P 10 -- I apologise if I misspoke. P 10406. All right. Well, it's in my -- if we could have it on -- if we could possibly have it on e-court, please. Sir, in the interest of time if you will --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I can be mistaken, but I don't think so. It is not a problem we don't have it in the binder, the problem is it is not on the chart. So it was not planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you can look on the screen and assist us. This is a -- this is a press article dated the 13th of July, 1992, and it goes back to topic that we touched on briefly earlier this afternoon, and that is that as of the 13th of July, 1992, and I'll just read the first sentence of the article: "Croatia said on Monday that it would not accept any more refugees from war-torn Bosnia-Herzegovina." And what can you tell us about that decision -- how that decision was made? And I will just indicate to you that at the top of the second page, at least in the English version, Mr. Zoric is quoted in this regard about this: "It is unbearable. Its not a question of goodwill. We don't have anywhere to put these people."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's been asked and answered. We already covered this ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Earlier, earlier today. Earlier today he was asked about the decision. He commented. He commented the reason, and he indicated that this was a plea but that the borders were never closed. That was during the first session. Now, we can go over it again, but I just want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands that this was asked and answered. Not this particular document but the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's the point, Your Honour. I'm coming back to a particular document on point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what more can you tell us looking at this document about the decision on the 13th of July, 1992, not to accept any more refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I really can't remember that the Republic of Croatia was ever in a situation to decide to close its borders with Bosnia and Herzegovina because it no longer wanted to receive refugees from that country. I did mention that that must have been a statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't say whether you wanted to or whether Croatia wanted to or not. The motivation is a separate issue at the moment. We have an article here and we have other testimony in the case that indeed there was a time when Croatia stopped accepting refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, can you tell us more about that -- did you make that decision? Was that a decision that you made, or who in the government made that decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I point to the earlier testimony of the gentleman. He indicated that the border was never closed, that they never refused refugees. He indicated that clearly in relation to this particular decision. Now he's being pointed -- he's being pointed an article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes I am. I'm challenging the witness, Your Honour. I don't have to accept his first answer. I can challenge the witness. This is cross-examination. That's what cross-examination is about. I put documents in front of him. I have other documents to put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, but we have a press clipping. That's the point. The press clipping is hearsay first of all. We don't have access to this particular individual. We don't know what this individual had in mind when he wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, press clippings have been coming into for the last two years. Now, are we changing the rules here now, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So am I understanding that what Mr. Scott is doing, he's putting his case to the witness that the witness indeed is a liar? Is that what Mr. Scott is doing because the answer has been answered -- the question has been answered earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please stop conducting legal or judicial guerrilla here in this courtroom. We have a press statement coming from Reuters, a very famous agency that does not just publish any -- anything. This relates to a statement made by the senior secretary of the office, and Mr. Zoric mentions financial problems. It might be relevant to find out why he made that statement. This will not cause any prejudice to your case. Furthermore, this is taking place in Croatia, not in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Scott, please proceed if you believe that we should expand some portion of -- a portion of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me see if I can move us forward and then maybe put additional questions to you, but in light of the comments that have been made, if I can direct your attention back to 1D 02008, the first exhibit we looked at this afternoon in the Prosecution's cross-examination. 1D 02008. Binder 1 of the Defence documents. I don't have them. I don't have -- my documents aren't organised in the same way as the Defence. Do you have it now, sir? Dr. Rebic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look on the screen. This is the document that we looked at. This is the record -- the letter that Mr. Prlic had sent to Dr. Granic about their meeting, the letter dated the 21st of November, 1992, which we've already looked at. And if I can direct your attention to the text of the enclosure, item number 1, item number 1 and mindful that this is written in November 1992: "In connection with refugees, it was stressed that Croatia does not have the physical, social, or material capabilities to receive a new wave of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina that is expected. The only possibility is transit to other countries." Now, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that an accurate statement as of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an accurate statement. The Republic of Croatia at the time had been exhausted. It did not have the physical, social, and material capabilities to receive a new wave of refugees. However, despite all that, we still received them because we made do as best as we could. I mentioned on several occasions that we asked from the Ministry of Defence to provide us with new capabilities that he had used to belong to the JNA. That's where we accommodated refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, there's one thing when is somebody on behalf of the Republic of Croatia talks in order to raise awareness amongst the others and tell them about physical incapabilities of accommodating refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it's a totally different thing that de facto we never turned down refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina when they crossed the Croatian border and arrived in Croatia. I don't remember a single event in which the ODPR turned down a refugee who came for help from the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I simply cannot remember any such event. And this is something that I understand as a cry out to the general public to sense -- to raise their awareness and to try and look to Bosnia and Herzegovina and see whether they themselves could deal with the problem of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Taking for purposes of argument that additional persons were physically allowed into Croatia, across its border, assuming that for the moment, we can debate that later, but assuming that was the case, was it nonetheless the position of the Croatian government if those people did come in after the 13th of July, 1992, they were not being given refugee status? They may have been physically there and they may have been good people who tried to assist them, but they were not given legal refugee status after the 13th of July, 1992. Now, is that what you're saying? Is that what this decision was saying?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, no. According to the talks in Grude, if I understand you correctly, on the 20th of November, 1992, these were talks in which Granic pointed out the impossibility or the difficulties --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm going to ask you now to go 1D 02608. It's in the Prosecution bundle I'm told. 1D 02608. Sorry, it's in the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. We're in the same situation as everybody else, I'm afraid. There are so many binders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "One time financial assistance"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. If I can ask you please to look to paragraph numbered 1 of your letter dated the -- or report or what have you dated 29th of October, 1992. In number one: "To strictly obey the stipulations of the Government of the Republic of Croatia as regards approving or non-approving the refugee status to those refugees who have arrived to Croatia before July 13, 1992. It is because there have been some irregularities." Now, you're writing this document some months later on the 29th of October, 1992. You're nonetheless referring to 13th of July, 1992, as the -- as a date having some significance. So why are you referring -- why in October 1992 are you referring back to -- why is it significant whether they have arrived before 13 July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave I think there is a mistranslation of this document, because in the Croatian text it speaks of refugees who arrived in Croatia after the 13th of July, 1992, and it says in the translation "before the 13th of July, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if our -- I'm sorry. I apologise. If our interpreters can assist us, I'll certainly be -- I will be governed by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, Ms. Alaburic, the best way to proceed is that you read that paragraph in your own language, paragraph 1, and the interpreters will be able to tell us if it was after or before. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence begins, I quote: "We asked the regional offices to request all centres for social work to: "1. To strictly obey the stipulations of the government of the Republic of Croatia as regards approving or non-approving of refugee status to those refugees who arrived in Croatia after the 13th of July, 1992. There have been some irregularities, that is."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this text should read after and not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully accept that, and I -- just for the record, this is a Defence exhibit and apparently a translation is in error, but really doesn't in fact -- but doesn't dramatically change my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You still refer, sir, to a decision on the 13th of July 1992, whether having a significance, maybe it was significant because something happened before that date or it was significant because something happened after that date, but you still tie this to the July 13, 1992. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today after all this time I cannot recall the significance of the 13th of July. However, I see from this document, which I believe I signed, although I don't see my signature here, and it has to do with a one-time financial assistance to hosts of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this document, the regional offices are asked to deliver to the office a list of all the hosts and the number of Bosnian-Herzegovinian refugees they are taking in so that we can provide them with one-time financial assistance of a certain sum per person, and also requests of the families taking in refugees and refugees asking for one-time financial assistance should be given this assistance only if they show the requisite documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'd like to move forward unless the Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Scott, before you move on to something else, I once again read paragraph 1, and I also wondered, just like yourself, about the same things, but if you read paragraph 1, one is under the impression that the witness sends an order to regional offices regarding this issue, and he asks them to strictly obey the stipulations or orders issued by the government of the Republic of Croatia as regards approving or non-approving the refugee status to those refugees who have arrived after the 13th of July. So when one reads this sentence, one is under the impression that on behalf of the government of the Republic of Croatia there is not a total refusal with regard to the people who arrived after the 13th of July, because there is this issue of approving or non-approving the refugee status. In other words, both options seem to exist. So, Witness, is this how we should interpret this paragraph, because this seems to stem from your own office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with you. That is how it should be interpreted, because at that time there were false cards showing refugee status, just as there were forged documents testifying to displaced person status. That's why I'm saying that the provisions should be respected as to who had the right and who did not have the right to that status, because this has to do with financial assistance which is not small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, but the end of the sentence seems to indicate that you discovered that there were some false refugees, in brackets, and that's why you're telling regional centres there have been some irregularities, but you've told us already, and we'd just like you to confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
